passage: Kofi came home from school in Accra and dropped his bag by the door. “How was the test?” his older sister Dalia asked. “Fine.” “Did you eat lunch?” “Yes.” “Was Yaw there?” “No.” Each answer was short and flat, and he headed straight for his room. Dalia opened her mouth to ask more, then stopped. She thought he might be tired, or hurt about something, or just not ready. Instead she made two cups of hot chocolate, set one outside his door, and said, “I'm on the balcony if you want to talk.” Half an hour later, Kofi came out and sat down beside her.

qa.q: Where did Dalia sit after leaving the cup outside Kofi's door?
qa.a: On the balcony.

qa.q: What did Dalia think Kofi's short answers might mean?
qa.a: She thought he might be tired, hurt about something or not ready to talk yet.

qa.q: Why was Dalia's plan better than asking more questions?
qa.a: It gave him time and a low-pressure moment, so he could come to her when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Kofi have felt about being asked so many questions right after school?
qa.a: He may have felt tired and wanted a quiet moment, so the questions could have felt like pressure.

grounding: Clipped replies after a hard day may mean tiredness, hurt or unreadiness, and offering time works better than demanding detail.

passage: After the afternoon bell, Akash walked into the school counselling room and dropped into a chair. Ms. Aparna asked, “How did the match go?” “Okay.” “Did you play well?” “Yeah.” “And your friends?” “Fine.” His replies were short, and he looked at the wall. She waited and then said, “You don't have to tell me now. I have some crayons and paper if you'd like to draw, and I'll be here till four.” Akash shrugged, but pulled the crayons over. Ten minutes later, without looking up, he said, “Ravi didn't pass me the ball all day.” Ms. Aparna nodded.

qa.q: How long did Ms. Aparna say she would be there?
qa.a: Until four.

qa.q: What might Akash have been feeling when he gave clipped answers?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt about the match and not ready to talk, which explains why he only shared later about the ball.

qa.q: What did Ms. Aparna do that made it easier for Akash to share?
qa.a: She stopped pushing for detail and offered crayons and time, so he could talk when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Ravi's behaviour look to Akash, compared with how Ravi might see it?
qa.a: Akash felt left out of the game, while Ravi may not have realised his passing left Akash hurt.

grounding: A child with clipped answers after a hard match may be hurt or unready to talk, and the counsellor offers time.

passage: I'm Manoj, from the flat next door, and I was pumping my cycle tyre on the landing when Hafsa came home from school. Her Ammi opened the door. “How was the test?” “Fine.” “Did you eat your lunch?” “Yes.” “And the bus?” “Okay.” Hafsa walked straight in and dropped her bag. I thought her Ammi would push, like mine does. She didn't. She just said, “There's chai when you want it,” and went back to the kitchen. About half an hour later, through the open window, I heard Hafsa's voice, long and wobbly, telling her Ammi everything about the test. I don't know what happened in it, but she was talking.

qa.q: What was Manoj doing on the landing?
qa.a: Manoj was pumping a cycle tyre.

qa.q: What was Hafsa likely feeling when she gave one-word answers?
qa.a: Hafsa was likely tired or upset after the test and not ready to talk yet.

qa.q: Why did Ammi's response work?
qa.a: She didn't demand details but offered chai and time, so Hafsa could come and talk when ready.

qa.q: How does Manoj compare Hafsa's Ammi with Manoj's own mother?
qa.a: Manoj expected Ammi to push the way Manoj's mother does, and was surprised she gave Hafsa space.

grounding: Shows a child's clipped replies after a hard day, and an adult offering time and a low-pressure moment instead of demanding detail.

passage: Monday: Sonali came in from dance class and answered every question with one word. “Good.” “No.” “Tired.” Rehana Khala kept asking. “What happened? Tell me. Why are you like this?” Sonali shut her bedroom door. Tuesday: Rehana didn't ask anything. After dinner she said, “I'm walking to the shop for milk. Want to come?” They walked in silence past the lit-up shops. Near the paan stall, Sonali said, “They took me out of the front row for the show.” Rehana just listened. Thursday: Sonali practised her steps in the living room and asked Rehana to watch.

qa.q: What did Rehana walk to the shop for?
qa.a: Rehana walked to the shop for milk.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling behind her one-word answers on Monday?
qa.a: She was hurt and disappointed about being taken out of the front row, and not ready to talk.

qa.q: What changed on Tuesday that helped Sonali open up?
qa.a: Rehana stopped questioning and offered a quiet walk, a low-pressure moment when Sonali could talk if she wanted.

qa.q: What would change if Rehana had kept pushing on Tuesday?
qa.a: Sonali might have stayed behind her closed door and never shared the hurt about the dance show.

grounding: Shows an adult learning that a child's clipped replies need time and a low-pressure moment rather than demands for detail.

passage: Vidya, when you say “fine” like that, I hear your mother at eleven. Let your Shankar Thatha tell you. One week she came home and every answer was clipped. “Fine.” “Nothing.” “Don't know.” I kept pushing, and she kept closing like a door. Then your Paati told me, “Stop asking. Just be there.” So one evening I sat on the steps oiling my cycle chain and said nothing. She came and sat, and after a long while she told me some girls had been calling her names because of her glasses. I thanked her for telling me. The same evening I phoned her class teacher, who spoke to those girls the very next morning.

qa.q: What was Thatha oiling on the steps?
qa.a: He was oiling his cycle chain.

qa.q: What was the girl feeling behind her clipped answers?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed by the name-calling about her glasses and not ready to talk.

qa.q: What choice did Thatha make after Paati's advice, and why did it work?
qa.a: He stopped asking and simply sat near her, a low-pressure moment that let her share the problem, and then he phoned her teacher that evening.

qa.q: How did Paati see the situation?
qa.a: Paati could see the pushing was making things worse and that the girl needed time and quiet company.

grounding: Shows a parent learning that a child's clipped replies need a low-pressure moment, not demands, and acting the same day on what she shared.

passage:
The power went out just as Elizabeth started the dal, so she was cooking by torchlight when Ira came in and dropped her bag.

"How was school, love?" "Fine."
"And the spelling test?" "Okay."
"Did you eat your lunch?" "Yeah."

Each answer was shorter than the one before. Elizabeth almost said, "Tell me properly!" Instead she held out the torch. "Can you shine this on the pot for me? My hands are full."

Ira held it. For a while there was only the hiss of the cooker and the torch beam wobbling. Then, very quietly: "Sanya said I can't sit with them any more."

Elizabeth kept stirring. "That sounds like it hurt. Tell me whenever you want."

qa.q: What did Elizabeth ask Ira to shine the torch on?
qa.a: The pot.

qa.q: What was Ira likely feeling behind the shorter and shorter answers?
qa.a: Hurt and upset about Sanya leaving her out, and not ready to talk yet; she may also have been tired after school.

qa.q: Which choice helped Ira open up?
qa.a: Elizabeth didn't demand details; she gave Ira a small job with the torch, a low-pressure moment side by side, until Ira was ready.

qa.q: What was it like for Elizabeth to get one-word answers in the middle of a power cut?
qa.a: She was busy and tempted to snap "Tell me properly!", but she held back, stayed calm and let the quiet do the work.

grounding: It shows a child giving clipped answers after a hurtful day, and a parent offering time and a low-pressure moment instead of demanding detail.
